projects.title: LED Blinking
projects.objective: Control an external LED on a digital output pin with a configurable blink timing interval, then extend it to a custom heartbeat pattern.
learningSequence: Declare a const int for the LED pin and timing interval.
Configure the pin as OUTPUT inside setup().
Alternate HIGH and LOW states inside loop() with delay().
Upgrade the timing using millis() once you finish Module 10 Lesson 9.
logicSteps: Choose a digital pin (e.g., pin 8) and store it in a named constant.
Configure the pin direction once in setup() using pinMode().
Turn the LED ON, wait 500 ms, turn the LED OFF, wait 500 ms.
Modify the ON and OFF durations to create an asymmetric beacon (200 ms ON, 800 ms OFF).
hardwareNotes: 1x LED (long leg = anode +, flat side/short leg = cathode -).
1x 220-ohm to 330-ohm current-limiting resistor in series with the LED (never omit the resistor).
Connect LED anode through resistor to Digital Pin 8; connect cathode to GND.
ideSteps: Download the starter skeleton below and open it in Arduino IDE.
Replace each TODO comment with your own Arduino C++ statements.
Select your board and port, click Verify to check syntax, then Upload.
projects.expectedHardwareBehavior: The external LED on Pin 8 flashes briefly for 0.2 seconds, stays off for 0.8 seconds, and repeats continuously.
projects.logicHint: Inside setup(), call pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);. Inside loop(), pair digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH); with delay(ON_TIME_MS);, then LOW with delay(OFF_TIME_MS);.

projects.title: Traffic Light System
projects.objective: Design a 3-LED sequential state controller (Green -> Yellow -> Red) using clean helper functions instead of repetitive code.
learningSequence: Map each light state (Green, Yellow, Red) on paper with exact durations.
Write a reusable function setLights(bool r, bool y, bool g) to guarantee only intended LEDs are lit.
Call your function in sequence inside loop().
logicSteps: Define three const int pins: RED_PIN, YELLOW_PIN, GREEN_PIN.
Set all three pins as OUTPUT inside setup().
Write a helper function that explicitly sets all three LEDs to HIGH or LOW.
Cycle Green (4000 ms) -> Yellow (1500 ms) -> Red (4000 ms) cleanly.
hardwareNotes: 3x LEDs (Red, Yellow, Green) and 3x 220-ohm resistors (one resistor per LED).
Wire LEDs to pins 10 (Red), 9 (Yellow), 8 (Green) with all cathodes tied to common GND.
ideSteps: Open the starter skeleton in Arduino IDE.
Complete the setLights() function so it updates all three pins deterministically.
Verify and upload; confirm no two lights stay accidentally stuck ON.
projects.expectedHardwareBehavior: Green lights for 4 seconds, transitions to Yellow for 1.5 seconds, then Red for 4 seconds, repeating smoothly.
projects.logicHint: Inside setLights(), you can write digitalWrite(RED_PIN, redOn ? HIGH : LOW); for each LED so every transition clears the previous light.

projects.title: Button-Controlled LED
projects.objective: Read a physical push button using INPUT_PULLUP and toggle an LED state cleanly when pressed, understanding active-LOW logic and contact bounce.
learningSequence: Learn why floating inputs cause random flickering and how INPUT_PULLUP solves it.
Detect a button press (LOW when wired to GND).
Track previous button state to toggle the LED once per press instead of flickering rapidly.
logicSteps: Configure the button pin with pinMode(BTN_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP).
Create boolean variables ledState and lastButtonState.
Detect a HIGH -> LOW transition (falling edge) when the button is pressed.
Flip ledState = !ledState, write it to the LED, and debounce with a short 30–50 ms pause.
hardwareNotes: 1x Tactile push button wired between Digital Pin 2 and GND (no external resistor needed with INPUT_PULLUP).
1x LED + 220-ohm resistor wired to Digital Pin 8 and GND.
ideSteps: Download the starter skeleton and open it in Arduino IDE.
Implement edge detection inside loop() so holding the button does not repeatedly toggle the LED.
Upload and test pressing, holding, and releasing the button.
projects.expectedHardwareBehavior: Each distinct press of the button cleanly toggles the LED between ON and OFF without flickering while held down.
projects.logicHint: Compare lastBtnReading == HIGH && currentReading == LOW inside an if statement, then set ledState = !ledState; digitalWrite(LED_PIN, ledState ? HIGH : LOW); delay(40);.

projects.title: Automatic Streetlight
projects.objective: Use an LDR (photoresistor) voltage divider on an analog pin to switch a streetlight LED automatically at dusk, adding hysteresis so it never flickers at twilight.
learningSequence: Read raw LDR values in the Serial Monitor under room light and covered by your hand.
Choose separate DARK_THRESHOLD and BRIGHT_THRESHOLD values (hysteresis band).
Switch the LED ON only below DARK_THRESHOLD and OFF only above BRIGHT_THRESHOLD.
logicSteps: Print analogRead(A0) values to Serial Monitor to calibrate your real room lighting.
Define DARK_THRESHOLD (e.g., 350) and BRIGHT_THRESHOLD (e.g., 450).
Use if (lightVal < DARK_THRESHOLD) to turn ON and else if (lightVal > BRIGHT_THRESHOLD) to turn OFF.
Leave the light state unchanged inside the 350–450 buffer band.
hardwareNotes: 1x LDR + 1x 10k-ohm resistor wired as a voltage divider between 5V (or 3.3V on ESP32) and GND, midpoint to A0.
ideSteps: Open the skeleton in Arduino IDE and upload.
Open Tools -> Serial Monitor at 9600 baud and observe readings in bright vs dark conditions.
Adjust your two threshold constants to match your sensor circuit.
projects.expectedHardwareBehavior: Covering the LDR turns the lamp ON steadily; uncovering it turns the lamp OFF without rapid flickering near dusk.
projects.logicHint: Check if (lightLevel < DARK_THRESHOLD) { digitalWrite(LAMP_PIN, HIGH); } else if (lightLevel > BRIGHT_THRESHOLD) { digitalWrite(LAMP_PIN, LOW); }.

projects.title: Buzzer Alarm
projects.objective: Trigger a two-tone audible alarm pattern using a piezo buzzer and for-loops when a trip button or sensor threshold is activated.
learningSequence: Distinguish passive buzzers (need tone() frequency) from active buzzers (need HIGH/LOW).
Write a soundAlarmCycle() function using a for loop to alternate two frequencies.
Trigger the alarm only when the alarm sensor input is active.
logicSteps: Declare BUZZER_PIN and SENSOR_BTN_PIN.
Create a helper function soundAlarm(int cycles) using a for loop.
Inside the loop, alternate tone(BUZZER_PIN, 880, 150) and tone(BUZZER_PIN, 1320, 150).
Call noTone(BUZZER_PIN) when the sensor is clear.
hardwareNotes: 1x Passive piezo buzzer connected between Digital Pin 6 and GND (optional 100-ohm resistor in series).
1x Trigger push button or reed switch between Digital Pin 2 and GND (INPUT_PULLUP).
ideSteps: Complete the soundAlarm() loop in Arduino IDE.
Upload and trigger the input switch to verify the two-tone alert stops cleanly when released.
projects.expectedHardwareBehavior: Pressing the trigger switch produces a clear alternating two-tone alarm; releasing it silences the buzzer.
projects.logicHint: Inside the for loop: tone(BUZZER_PIN, 880); delay(160); tone(BUZZER_PIN, 1320); delay(160); followed by noTone(BUZZER_PIN); after the loop.

projects.title: Ultrasonic Distance Meter
projects.objective: Measure real-world object distance in centimeters using an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, pulseIn(), and floating-point math, printing clean readings to the Serial Monitor.
learningSequence: Understand how sound travels to an object and echoes back (divide round-trip distance by 2).
Send a clean 10-microsecond HIGH trigger pulse.
Measure echo duration with pulseIn(ECHO_PIN, HIGH, 30000) timeout so the program never hangs.
Return distance in cm from a dedicated measureDistanceCm() function.
logicSteps: Write a function float measureDistanceCm() that sends a 10 us pulse on TRIG_PIN.
Capture unsigned long duration = pulseIn(ECHO_PIN, HIGH, 30000UL).
Handle timeout (duration == 0) by returning -1.0f.
Convert microseconds to centimeters using (duration * 0.0343f) / 2.0f and print to Serial Monitor.
hardwareNotes: 1x HC-SR04 Ultrasonic Sensor (VCC -> 5V, GND -> GND, TRIG -> Pin 9, ECHO -> Pin 10 on 5V Uno/Mega).
If using a 3.3V board (ESP32 / Nano ESP32), place a 1k/2k resistor voltage divider on ECHO so it never sends 5V into a 3.3V GPIO.
ideSteps: Complete measureDistanceCm() in Arduino IDE and upload.
Open Serial Monitor (9600 baud) and place a flat book 10 cm, 20 cm, and 30 cm in front of the sensor to verify accuracy.
projects.expectedHardwareBehavior: Serial Monitor prints accurate distance measurements in centimeters every 200 ms and reports 'Out of range' when pointed at open space.
projects.logicHint: Use digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, LOW); delayMicroseconds(2); digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, HIGH); delayMicroseconds(10); digitalWrite(TRIG_PIN, LOW); before calling pulseIn().

projects.title: Servo Controller
projects.objective: Map a potentiometer's analog reading smoothly to a servo angle (0 to 180 degrees) using the standard Servo library and constrain() safety bounds.
learningSequence: Include <Servo.h> and instantiate a Servo object.
Attach the servo signal wire to a PWM-capable pin in setup().
Read the potentiometer, map 0–1023 to 10–170 degrees (avoiding mechanical end-stop strain), and write the angle.
logicSteps: Include <Servo.h> and create Servo armServo;
Call armServo.attach(SERVO_PIN) inside setup().
Read potValue = analogRead(POT_PIN) in loop().
Map and constrain the angle between 10 and 170 degrees before calling armServo.write(angle).
hardwareNotes: 1x Micro Servo (SG90 or similar): Signal -> Pin 9, GND -> Common GND.
For larger servos or multiple servos, power VCC from an external 5V supply (never pull heavy servo stall current from the Arduino 5V regulator) and connect grounds together.
1x 10k Potentiometer: outer legs to 5V & GND, center wiper to A0.
ideSteps: Complete the map(), constrain(), and armServo.write() lines in Arduino IDE.
Upload and slowly rotate the potentiometer to verify smooth, jitter-free angular tracking.
projects.expectedHardwareBehavior: Turning the potentiometer knob smoothly rotates the servo horn proportionally between 10 and 170 degrees.

projects.title: Obstacle Detection
projects.objective: Combine an ultrasonic sensor with a motor-driver state machine (Forward, Stop, Turn) so a two-wheel robot autonomously avoids obstacles closer than 20 cm.
learningSequence: Build and test clean motor helper functions first: driveForward(), stopMotors(), turnRight().
Integrate your tested measureDistanceCm() function.
Write a clear decision loop: if valid distance < SAFE_DISTANCE_CM -> stop, turn, re-check; else drive forward.
logicSteps: Define left/right motor direction pins for your H-bridge driver (e.g., L298N or TB6612FNG).
Write modular movement functions so loop() reads like plain English.
Ignore invalid timeouts (distance <= 0) so false zero readings do not trigger phantom stops.
When distance > 0 && distance < 20.0f, call stopMotors(), pause briefly, turnRight(), and resume scanning.
hardwareNotes: NEVER connect DC motors directly to Arduino GPIO pins — always use an H-bridge motor driver (L298N, L293D, or TB6612FNG).
Power the motor driver from a dedicated battery pack (e.g., 6V–9V) and tie battery GND to Arduino GND.
Mount the HC-SR04 facing forward at chassis height.
ideSteps: Test your motor functions on a raised stand (wheels off the ground) before placing the robot on the floor.
Complete the obstacle decision branch inside loop() and verify responses with a flat obstacle.
projects.expectedHardwareBehavior: The robot drives forward when the path is clear; when an object appears closer than 20 cm, it halts, pivots right to clear the obstacle, and resumes driving.
projects.logicHint: Always guard with (dist > 0 && dist < SAFE_CM) so an out-of-range -1.0f reading is treated as clear space rather than an obstacle.
